basic_identification.name: Post-internet art 2.0
basic_identification.originator: Second wave builds on Marisa Olson (coined 'postinternet' 2006), Artie Vierkant ('The Image Object Post-Internet' 2010), Gene McHugh, DIS collective. Current voices: Holly Herndon, Mat Dryhurst, Jon Rafman, Avery Singer, Simon Denny, Legacy Russell, Anika Meier
basic_identification.geography: Global, centered in New York, Berlin, London, Los Angeles. Exhibition circuits in Europe, North America, Asia

core_ideas.core_claim: The first wave of post-internet art celebrated or ironically engaged with network culture and platform aesthetics. The second wave (post-2022) updates this critique for conditions of AI ubiquity, platform decay, post-NFT disillusionment, and technofeudalism. Art now confronts not the novelty of the internet but its inescapability, its capture mechanisms, and the rise of AI as a creative and economic force that artists cannot ignore but must critically engage.
core_ideas.medium_specificity: Operates across digital and physical media, insisting that the distinction is obsolete. The first wave explored the image-object duality (Vierkant); the second wave contends with AI-generated imagery, synthetic media, deepfakes, and the collapse of photographic truth. The digital specificity lies in engaging with algorithmic mediation as the dominant condition of cultural production, not as a chosen medium.
core_ideas.relation_to_attention_economy: Critical but embedded. First-wave post-internet art used attention as currency (Vierkant's 'universal authorship' thesis). The second wave is more skeptical, responding to what Yanis Varoufakis calls technofeudalism — the capture of attention by platform monopolies. Artists like Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst develop alternative models (Spawning, Holly+) that resist attention extraction while operating within its structures. The tension between critique and complicity is central to the movement.
core_ideas.relation_to_intention: Mixed. The critical discourse is intention-oriented (developing frameworks for understanding AI, platform capitalism, post-truth conditions). But the movement circulates through art market channels (galleries, biennials, auction houses) that operate on attention logic. The Spike Art Magazine question 'What's after post-internet art?' reflects the movement's own uncertainty about whether it serves structural needs or generates market-friendly discourse.

market_economics.revenue_model: Gallery sales (primary market), auction sales, institutional acquisitions, commissions, speaking fees, writing. Some artists develop alternative revenue through technology ventures (Herndon/Dryhurst's Spawning AI, which raised venture capital). The AI art market reached $3.2 billion in 2024.
market_economics.market_position: Primary and secondary art markets. Major gallery representation (e.g., Avery Singer at Hauser & Wirth). Auction presence (Christie's first all-AI auction February 2025, grossing ~$730,000). Institutional collecting by major museums.
market_economics.price_range: Wide range: emerging artists $5,000-$50,000; established figures $100,000-$1,000,000+. Avery Singer's works have sold for over $1 million. Ai-Da robot artist sold at Sotheby's for over $1 million. [uncertain]
market_economics.volume_trend_2024_2026: Growing but bifurcated. AI art market expanding rapidly (projected $40.4 billion by 2033). But critical post-internet discourse is distinct from commercial AI art. The serious critical practice is stable; the AI-art-as-commodity sector is booming. The movement benefits from but is not identical to AI art market growth.
market_economics.collector_demographics: Mixed: traditional contemporary art collectors, tech-adjacent collectors, institutional buyers (museums, foundations). The AI art boom attracts crypto-adjacent and tech-industry collectors. Serious critical work appeals to institutional and established collectors. The market is more mainstream than first-wave post-internet art. [uncertain]
market_economics.sustainability: Moderate sustainability for the critical discourse. Academic positions, institutional commissions, and writing sustain the intellectual work. Gallery market sustains object-makers. The risk is that the term becomes meaningless through overuse (as happened with 'post-internet') or that market interest shifts to the next discourse. The underlying questions (how does art respond to AI?) are durable even if the label is not.

practice_aesthetics.toolchain: Diverse and medium-agnostic. AI tools (Stable Diffusion, DALL-E, Midjourney, custom models), 3D printing, CNC fabrication, traditional painting and sculpture, video, installation, web-based works, social media interventions, smart contracts. The toolchain reflects the movement's refusal to privilege any single medium.
practice_aesthetics.relation_to_AI: Central. AI is simultaneously medium, subject, collaborator, and threat. First-wave post-internet artists used Photoshop and the browser; second-wave artists use or critically engage with generative AI. Holly Herndon trained custom voice models (Holly+). Jon Rafman uses AI image generation to explore dream logic and digital uncanny. Avery Singer paints from AI-generated compositions. The movement's relationship to AI is not adoption or rejection but critical entanglement.
practice_aesthetics.liveness: Varied. Includes static artifacts (paintings, sculptures, prints), real-time installations, performative works, evolving online projects, and generative systems. The liveness question is less about format and more about temporal urgency — as Jon Rafman noted, the meaning of AI art shifts faster than exhibitions can keep up.
practice_aesthetics.aesthetic_vocabulary: Rich but contested. Inherits from first-wave post-internet (post-internet, network culture, image-object, circulation, attention economy) and adds: post-AI, synthetic media, technofeudalism, devirtualization, protocol aesthetics, prompt culture, latent space. ArtReview, Spike, e-flux, and Frieze are key venues for this discourse. The vocabulary is still forming around AI-specific conditions. Critics note the term 'post-internet' already felt exhausted by 2016; 'post-AI' may face similar entropy.
practice_aesthetics.tendency_axis_position: Internally divided on all axes. The critical discourse tends toward openness, commons, and infrastructure (Herndon/Dryhurst's Spawning platform). The market dimension tends toward enclosure, capture, and spectacle (auction houses, gallery sales). Individual artists position differently. The movement as a whole occupies the tension between these poles rather than resolving it.

infrastructure_governance.openness: Hybrid. Critical writings circulate freely (ArtReview, e-flux, Spike). Some artists develop open tools (Holly+'s voice protocol). But gallery works are proprietary, edition-controlled. The movement does not have a unified stance on openness — it inherits the art market's enclosure logic while producing critical discourse about that enclosure.
infrastructure_governance.governance_model: No formal governance. The movement is shaped by curatorial decisions (biennials, museums, galleries), editorial gatekeeping (art magazines), and academic discourse. Individual artists and collectives make autonomous decisions. DIS operated as a loose collective; current practitioners are mostly individual studio practices with gallery representation.
infrastructure_governance.data_sovereignty: Uneven. Artists using AI tools face questions about training data sovereignty (whose images trained the model?). Herndon/Dryhurst's Spawning project specifically addresses this, allowing artists to opt out of AI training datasets. But most practitioners do not engage with data sovereignty questions at the infrastructure level. Gallery-sold works follow standard art market ownership norms.
infrastructure_governance.interoperability: Low to moderate. Works exist in diverse formats (physical objects, web projects, video, installation) without standardized infrastructure. No common API or data format. The movement is conceptually coherent but technically fragmented.
infrastructure_governance.preservation_strategy: Mixed. Physical works preserved through standard art conservation. Digital and web-based works face the same preservation challenges as all internet art — platform dependency, format obsolescence, link rot. Institutional acquisitions provide some preservation guarantee. Rhizome's preservation work covers some net art heritage but not the broader movement.
infrastructure_governance.consent_architecture: Emerging. Spawning's 'Have I Been Trained?' tool introduced opt-out consent for AI training data. This is the most significant consent architecture contribution from this movement. Otherwise, standard art market consent norms apply (exhibition agreements, reproduction rights). The broader question of consent in AI-mediated art production is actively debated but not systemically addressed.

field_position.relation_to_traditional_art_world: Deeply integrated. Unlike first-wave net art, post-internet art 2.0 operates within galleries, museums, biennials, and auction houses. The 2016 Berlin Biennale (curated by DIS) marked peak institutional absorption. Current practitioners show at major galleries and sell at auction. The movement critiques the art world from within it.
field_position.what_it_enables: Critical frameworks for understanding art in the age of AI. Vocabulary for discussing synthetic media, algorithmic mediation, and platform capitalism. Models for artist-led technology development (Spawning). A bridge between art criticism and technology ethics. Legitimation of digital and AI-engaged practice within the contemporary art establishment.
field_position.what_it_lacks: Consensus on what distinguishes serious critical practice from market-friendly AI art spectacle. Infrastructure for preserving born-digital works. Economic models that do not depend on traditional gallery structures. Diversity — the discourse remains dominated by Euro-American voices despite global digital conditions. A clear successor framework as 'post-internet' and 'post-AI' labels lose specificity.
field_position.who_is_excluded: Artists without gallery representation or institutional connections. Practitioners from the Global South whose experiences of platform capitalism differ from Euro-American frameworks. Non-English speakers (discourse is overwhelmingly English-language). Artists who engage with digital culture but reject the theoretical framing of 'post-internet.' Working-class artists who cannot sustain the research-intensive, low-immediate-return practice model. [uncertain]
field_position.frontier_signal: Established movement with frontier discourse. The first wave is historical (2008-2016). The second wave is actively developing critical frameworks for AI, post-NFT, and platform decay conditions. The frontier question is whether this discourse produces lasting critical tools or becomes another exhausted art-world label.

attention_intention.discovery_mechanism: Art publications (ArtReview, Frieze, e-flux, Spike, Artforum), gallery exhibitions, biennials, museum shows, social media (Instagram, Twitter/X), academic conferences, art fairs. Algorithm-mediated discovery through Instagram is significant for younger artists.
attention_intention.attention_dependency: Moderate to high. The movement depends on art-world attention infrastructure (reviews, exhibitions, social media circulation). Gallery careers require visibility. However, the critical discourse could survive platform disappearance through publications, books, and academic channels. The commercial dimension is more attention-dependent than the intellectual one.
attention_intention.intention_alignment: Split. The critical discourse is intention-aligned (building frameworks, developing vocabulary, creating tools like Spawning). The market dimension is attention-aligned (gallery sales, auction performance, social media presence). This internal split is the movement's central contradiction and, arguably, its productive tension.
attention_intention.commons_contribution: Moderate. Critical essays and theoretical frameworks are published openly. Spawning's tools contribute to commons infrastructure. But gallery works are enclosed as private property. Academic publications may be paywalled. The movement contributes more to shared vocabulary than to shared technical infrastructure.

provenance_temporality.provenance_type: Mixed. Physical works track ownership provenance through gallery records. Some AI-generated works reference training data provenance (whose images contributed?). The movement is more interested in provenance of meaning — how the significance of a work changes as AI conditions evolve — than in ownership tracking.
provenance_temporality.temporal_logic: Anticipatory and rapidly shifting. Jon Rafman's observation that AI art from five years ago already feels more distant than early photography captures the temporal compression. The discourse is always looking ahead while trying to historicize a present that changes faster than criticism can keep up.
provenance_temporality.absence_handling: Strong on detecting absence. The movement identifies what is missing: adequate critical vocabulary for AI art, consent frameworks for training data, economic models beyond gallery speculation, non-Western perspectives on digital culture. The Spike Magazine question 'What's after post-internet art?' is itself an absence-detection mechanism.

coherence.coherence_vs_consensus: Coherence without consensus. The movement agrees that art must critically engage with AI and platform conditions but disagrees on how. Some embrace AI as medium (Rafman, Singer), others build alternative infrastructure (Herndon/Dryhurst), others maintain ironic distance. The ArtReview roundtable format — multiple artists in disagreement — embodies this coherence-through-dialogue approach.
coherence.contestability: High. The movement is defined by internal debate. Terms are constantly contested (Is 'post-AI' useful? Does 'post-internet' still mean anything?). Aesthetic judgments are debated across publications. The hashtags #ArtistRights and #NoToAI after Christie's AI auction show public contestation of the movement's commercial dimension.
coherence.forkability: High conceptually, moderate practically. Anyone can engage with the questions the movement raises. But participation in the art-world conversation requires institutional access (galleries, publications, biennials). The discourse can be forked; the market position cannot.

adai_comparison.what_adai_should_adopt: The movement's insistence on critical engagement with AI rather than naive adoption or blanket rejection. The Spawning model of building artist-controlled tools as infrastructure. The vocabulary development work — A(DAI) needs the conceptual tools this movement is forging. The attention to temporal compression — how meaning shifts rapidly in AI conditions.
adai_comparison.what_adai_should_refuse: The art market dependency that constrains critical independence. The tendency toward discursive exhaustion (term inflation without lasting analytical tools). The Euro-American centrism of the discourse. The acceptance of gallery enclosure as the default economic model while critiquing enclosure in other domains.
adai_comparison.structural_tension: Post-internet art 2.0 generates critical vocabulary but lacks infrastructure; A(DAI) builds infrastructure but needs critical vocabulary. The movement operates through attention-economy channels (galleries, publications) while A(DAI) aims to build intention-native infrastructure. The tension is between discourse-as-product (the movement) and infrastructure-as-practice (A(DAI)). A(DAI) can absorb the critical insights while rejecting the market dependency.

regulatory_legal.regulatory_exposure: Significant and growing. AI-generated art faces copyright questions under DMCA, EU AI Act, and AB 2013 (California AI transparency). The US Copyright Office has ruled that purely AI-generated images cannot be copyrighted. Artists using AI tools face uncertain IP status. Spawning's opt-out tool responds directly to the regulatory gap around training data consent. The movement is at the frontier of art-AI regulatory questions.
regulatory_legal.ip_model: Mixed. Gallery works follow traditional all-rights-reserved with gallery representation agreements. AI-generated works face unresolved IP questions. Spawning advocates for artist consent in AI training. Some artists use Creative Commons for digital works. The IP landscape is unsettled and actively contested.
regulatory_legal.opt_in_vs_opt_out: The movement highlights this question without resolving it. Spawning's 'Have I Been Trained?' is an opt-out tool (artists must actively refuse inclusion in training data). Holly Herndon advocates for opt-in consent models. The tension between opt-in and opt-out is a live debate within the movement, with implications for the entire AI art field.

ecosystem.platform_dependency: Moderate. Gallery careers depend on art market infrastructure (galleries, fairs, auction houses). Digital distribution depends on social media platforms. Critical discourse depends on publication platforms (art magazines, academic journals). No single point of failure, but the ecosystem is embedded in multiple platform dependencies.
ecosystem.network_effects: Strong within the art world. More critical discourse attracts more practitioners, more institutional attention, more market activity. The movement benefits from network effects within the contemporary art ecosystem. But it also faces saturation — too much discourse can devalue the label.
ecosystem.post_crash_trajectory: Pivoting and adapting. The 2022-2023 NFT crash discredited the speculative crypto-art market but validated the movement's critical stance. Anika Meier declared 'Post-Internet Art Is Dead! Long Live Post-NFT Art!' The movement absorbed the crash as evidence of its critique while pivoting to AI as the new terrain. Currently in a growth phase driven by AI discourse, with Christie's 2025 AI auction marking mainstream acceptance.
